messages.author: fecbe3dc811bed89
messages.subject: improve speed & reduce nodes
parts:
Dear NIMBLE authors,

I got a question about the speed of execution.

a) In test.R (for an item response theory model), I compare two methods-- one uses 'no nimbleFunction' (see Line 23-31) and the other uses nimbleFunction (see Line 34). Why using nimbleFunction made execution slower? Can we speed it up by any tricks?

b) Line 34 is simply an intermediate computation. Can we avoid this to speed up the execution?

Thank you in advance, and thanks a lot for developing this great MCMC software.

Keith

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: improve speed & reduce nodes
parts:
Hi Keith,

a) In general, it would be surprising that using a user-defined nimbleFunction is slower than having the calculation as part of your model directly. 
However, if using the nimbleFunction causes an increase in the number of dependencies when updating a given parameter, it could slow things down. I think that may be happening here - in the version without a nimbleFunction, if you update t[1] then only some of the nu and p values need to be recalculated. But with the nimbleFunction, all of the nu and p values are recalculated. 

Also, given 'point' is only 3, we wouldn't expect using a nimbleFunction to help much even if there wasn't the question of changing the number of dependencies.

b) I'm not sure how you would avoid the intermediate calculation, given that 'p' is a function of 't', 'tau', and 'alpha'. I may be misunderstanding what you are asking.

-chris

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: improve speed & reduce nodes
parts:
hi Keith,

a) I didn't take the time to see all of what is going on with dependencies, but my general comment still holds -- you want to write your model (and associated user-defined nimbleFunctions) in such a way that you avoid unnecessary dependencies. It looks like there are distinct parameters for each pair of {n,i} values that determine the likelihood for res[n,i]. Alternatively, if you do introduce additional dependencies, it may make sense to do block sampling.

b) You could write a user-defined distribution that both calculates 'p' and does the dcat calculation all at the same time, thereby avoiding having all the 'p' nodes.

-chris
